# The Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"The purpose of computing is insight, not numbers."*
>
> — Richard Hamming, *Numerical Methods for Scientists and Engineers* (1962) [@Hamming1962NumericalMethods]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Richard Hamming, a pioneer in computer science, argued that
computing should yield insight rather than raw data. The distinction matters
here. AI-assisted architecture should help architects ask better questions,
test alternatives, explain mechanisms, and defend decisions. Producing more
candidates is useful only when it improves that work.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
Computer architecture needs more than faster artifact generation. The
moonshot is a coordinated AI-assisted design capability that can turn a
compact system goal into a supported hardware-and-software architecture
result. What would such a result have to establish, and how would we know
whether AI improved the work?
:::

Computer architecture has repeatedly expanded what engineers could design by
changing its methods as well as its devices. AI is another possible
design-method change, not an assumed necessity or a guarantee of better
architecture. Its ability to work with less structured information, propose
and screen alternatives, and coordinate actions across tools makes the
possibility worth testing, but it does not make the resulting artifacts
correct, physically realizable, or architecturally useful. This chapter defines
that possibility as a moonshot and states the tests it would have to pass.

This chapter develops that ambition methodically. It first looks at earlier
changes in design method that expanded what engineers could build. It then
introduces the Lighthouse request, expands the few lines of that request into
a full-stack architecture problem, and establishes the difference between a
generated artifact and a supported result. The chapter closes by stating what
Architecture 2.0 changes, why the work must be deliberately coordinated, and
the two comparisons that would show whether the moonshot succeeded.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, you can:

- Explain how earlier changes in design methods expanded what engineers could
  design, and why AI-assisted architecture should be judged by the same
  standard.
- Translate a compact system request into workload, software, hardware,
  implementation, physical, and verification requirements.
- Distinguish a request, specification, artifact, candidate, measurement,
  architecture result, and design decision.
- Explain what learned models, predictors, generators, optimizers, retrieval,
  and agents can contribute without treating AI as one monolithic component.
- Apply separate tests to the architecture result and the contribution made by
  AI.

:::

## When New Methods Changed What Engineers Could Design

The most consequential advances in computing have not come only from better
components. They have also come from better ways to express, divide, check,
and reuse design work. The Mead--Conway VLSI methodology[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] joined abstractions
and design rules to tools, fabrication access, and teaching
[@MeadConway1980VLSI]. Reduced-instruction-set computing reshaped the
hardware--software contract around a small set of principles that architects
could test quantitatively [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. Logic synthesis made it
practical to transform register-transfer-level descriptions into gate-level
implementations while timing analysis and equivalence checking exposed bad
outputs [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization]. Each change expanded what
engineers could design because it combined an idea with a method that other
people could apply, inspect, and improve.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

These transformations used different technical mechanisms, but each widened
the unit of design that engineers could express and made the resulting object
checkable through shared rules, tools, or measurements
(@fig-design-method-progression).

![**New design methods widened what engineers could express and check.** Established advances joined an input abstraction to a larger design object and to the checks or infrastructure that made the transformation dependable. AI-assisted architecture is shown separately as a prospective system for carrying system intent and current project state to a supported architecture result through existing tools and checks.](images/F1d-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-alt="Historical progression through Mead-Conway design rules and abstractions, the RISC hardware-software contract, RTL logic synthesis, and reusable hardware generators. Each established method connects an input abstraction to a design object and a dependable check or infrastructure. A separate prospective panel shows an AI-assisted design system connecting system intent and current project state through existing tools and checks to a supported architecture result."}

Read the established examples from left to right. Mead--Conway connected
scalable abstractions and design rules to layout and fabrication access. RISC
made a simpler hardware--software contract testable through quantitative
evaluation. Logic synthesis connected RTL and constraints to gate-level
implementation through timing and equivalence checks. Reusable hardware
generators widened the design object from one implementation to a parameterized
family while retaining downstream simulation and implementation checks
[@Izraelevitz2017Chisel]. The prospective panel is deliberately separate. It
is not an inevitable next stage or a
prompt-to-chip pipeline. It asks whether a design system can connect broader
intent and current project state to a supported architecture result while
continuing to rely on established tools and checks.

That is the standard for the present moment. Generating more code, RTL, or
design proposals would be useful, but it would not by itself constitute a new
design method. The stronger opportunity is to help architects carry intent
across workloads, software, hardware, and physical implementation while
reducing the human effort required to explore and check alternatives. We call
that long-range target an *architecture moonshot*.

> **Architecture moonshot.** An architecture moonshot is a difficult,
> long-term target that existing tools and design practice cannot yet address
> end to end. It seeks a major improvement in how architects turn system and
> chip design questions into supported results and decisions. Advances in AI,
> data, or tools must make at least part of the target practical to investigate
> without implying that the whole problem has been solved.

An architecture moonshot joins three conditions: an important architecture
problem, a substantial change in design practice, and an enabling advance that
makes meaningful progress possible. @fig-moonshot-venn places the target at
their overlap.

![**The moonshot sits where all three conditions meet:** it combines a major architecture challenge, a substantial change in AI-assisted design work, and an advance in AI, data, or tools that makes part of the problem practical to study.](images/F1c-moonshot-venn){#fig-moonshot-venn width="85%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram showing an architecture moonshot at the intersection of a grand challenge, a radical practice target, and an enabling breakthrough."}

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Read the two upper circles as the problem and the proposed change in practice.
The lower circle supplies the AI, data, or tool advance that makes part of the
target testable. Only the center overlap qualifies. A difficult problem without
a new method remains an unsolved problem. A new method without a demonstrated
enabling capability remains an aspiration. The enabling advance is therefore
not something a program may simply assume.

Explicitly Parallel Instruction Computing (EPIC), the basis of Itanium, offers
a useful warning. It moved instruction scheduling from hardware to the
compiler and depended on static compilation exposing enough parallelism to
produce a general-purpose advantage [@SchlanskerRau2000EPIC].

::: {.callout-war-story title="The compiler breakthrough EPIC needed did not close the gap"}
**The claim.** EPIC promised a step change by exposing instruction-level
parallelism at compile time.

**The gap.** Memory latency, branches, aliasing, and other run-time behavior
limited how much parallelism a compiler could schedule statically.
Out-of-order superscalar processors improved while preserving the established
software path.

**The lesson.** A moonshot can fail when it depends on a capability whose
limits become clear only after large commitments. AI-assisted architecture
faces the same risk if it assumes that plausible generation will become
physically valid system design without demonstrating the required knowledge,
tool use, and checks.
:::

The lesson is not to avoid ambitious targets. It is to state what capability
the target depends on and what result would challenge that assumption. The
Lighthouse request introduced below gives this book a concrete architecture
problem on which to do both.

## AI as Design Automation

The field is now applying AI to the design processes that produce modern
processors and accelerators, targeting tasks from design-space exploration to
physical placement
[@WangEtAl2026AgentDSE; @MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. In this book,
*AI* serves as an umbrella term. It includes learned methods for prediction,
generation, optimization, and other task-specific uses, as well as systems
that combine those methods with conventional analysis and design tools.

A *learned model* fits part of its behavior from examples rather than having
every rule written explicitly. A *predictor* estimates a property that is
expensive or unavailable to measure directly. A *generator* proposes an
artifact or design candidate. An *optimizer* chooses among alternatives to
improve a stated objective. *Retrieval* finds relevant information in an
identified body of material. An *agent* takes actions in an environment,
observes what the environment returns, and can change its next action from
that feedback. A model that answers one prompt is not necessarily an agent,
and a fixed script is not an agent simply because it calls several tools.

These names describe capabilities, not authority. Generation, prediction, and
optimization are method families; proposing a candidate, estimating a
consequence, selecting an experiment, repairing an artifact, and checking a
property are roles. One method can perform several roles, and a role can be
filled by a learned method, a conventional algorithm, a design tool, or an
architect. A later methods chapter develops how to choose and combine these
families.

AI in architecture also has a longer history than recent generative systems.
Researchers have used learned predictors, surrogate models, reinforcement
learning, and autotuning for branch prediction, prefetching, controllers, and
design-space exploration [@ChenPenneyJimenez2020AIArchitecture;
@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE; @ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Recent language and
generative models broaden the kinds of information and artifacts that methods
can work with [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo; @HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. The continuity
matters. Architecture already combines human judgment with models, scripts,
generators, simulators, compilers, synthesis, optimization, and verification.
The new question is where learned methods improve that complete practice.

Applying these methods to architecture runs into two immediate limits. Much of
the high-fidelity hardware data stays proprietary, and model use adds
computational overhead, latency, and financial cost. Any claimed benefit must
therefore account for both the simulator or engineering work saved and the work
needed to check that a generated claim holds for the physical design.

## The Lighthouse Request

These limits become concrete when a short product request expands into work
across the full design stack. Consider the following design brief.

> **Lighthouse prompt.** Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an
> XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. Realize it as a vector-capable CPU, accelerator, or SoC block under a 3\ W TDP target in a 3\ nm-class LP mobile process, and return a design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives.

We call this the *Lighthouse prompt*. Here XR means extended reality, TDP means
thermal design power, and LP identifies a low-power process. XRBench is a public
suite of mobile XR workloads rather than a complete product specification
[@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. Among the public systems reviewed for this edition, none
establishes an end-to-end answer. The prompt's scale deliberately exposes
the architecture work that a smaller generation task would hide, providing a
long-term target for judging progress toward the full challenge. The prompt targets mobile XR
specifically because it forces simultaneous extreme constraints on latency,
thermal limits, and energy efficiency. It also forces cross-layer integration. An
accelerator block in an industrial SoC is not a clean-sheet island; it must
interface with legacy, black-box IP over rigid standard protocols (like AMBA
AXI)[^fn-axi-c01]. A proposed design is dead on arrival if it optimizes power,
performance, and area (PPA) but drops an AXI handshake.

[^fn-axi-c01]: **AMBA AXI**: An Arm-defined on-chip interface protocol with separate channels and strict valid-ready handshake requirements [@Arm2020AXI]. A block that violates the protocol cannot be integrated into a system that depends on that interface, no matter how good its isolated power and performance numbers look.

The word *prompt* is intentionally modest. A request or prompt expresses
compact intent. Requirements interpret its obligations and identify choices
that remain open. A specification fixes enough behavior, interfaces, workloads,
software semantics, constraints, alternatives, and acceptance checks to make a
comparison possible. The Lighthouse request is not yet a specification.
"XRBench-class," "3\ W," "3\ nm-class," and the permitted compute organizations
still require versioned workloads, software paths, reference designs, process
assumptions, and checks.

The architect must make those choices explicit before the request can guide
real design work. AI may help interpret documents, retrieve relevant
information, propose requirements, or expose ambiguities. The architect still
decides which interpretation becomes part of the specification and what result
would satisfy it.

The prompt does not imply a single model or invocation. Answering it takes an XRBench trace, a compiler that can target whatever the proposal invents, a simulator, a synthesis run against a low-power library, and a reviewer who can say which of those results the recommendation actually rests on. What this book studies is that whole assembly and the decision it supports, not the fluency of any single generated response.

That system boundary requires *architecture* and *architect* to be explicit.
Architecture is more than a microarchitecture, block diagram, or chip artifact.

> **Architecture.** Architecture is the hardware and software contract and system organization turning workload intent and technology constraints into a defensible system design. It includes the instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory, interconnects, accelerators, chiplets, compiler interfaces, physical-design constraints, verification plans, deployment models, and the evidence used to justify choices.

> **Architect.** The architect is the owner of the decision. The architect frames the problem, chooses abstractions, sets the evidence standard, defines what disqualifies a candidate, and remains answerable for the committed design. While one person may hold this role or a team may divide the work, the division must explicitly state who holds decision and approval authority. Methods can contribute candidates and analysis, but the architect remains responsible for synthesizing the results into a recommendation and defending the ultimate architectural claim.

These definitions set the scope of the Lighthouse answer. It must cover the
hardware and software system, and an architect must be able to defend the
resulting recommendation.

The Lighthouse request fixes the workload class, 64-bit RISC-V basis, permitted
compute organizations, 3\ W envelope, 3\ nm-class low-power process, and the
required comparative report. A particular investigation must still fix the
workload version and deadline, architecture and software path, reference
design, process libraries, operating assumptions, tools, budget, and stopping
conditions. Changing a fixed condition changes the challenge; resolving an
open choice makes the challenge executable.

## From a Few Lines to a Full-Stack Problem {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

The Lighthouse request spans the entire stack because its compact wording
conceals two levels of work. Its phrases must first become architecture
requirements and then a tool-connected comparison that can support a decision
(@fig-moonshot-prompt).

![**A compact prompt hides a full architecture study.** The prompt implies architecture requirements and engineering work that must be completed before an architect can turn it into a supported result and decision.](images/F1-moonshot-stack){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="85%" fig-alt="Stacked diagram with the full Lighthouse prompt at the top, architecture requirements in the middle, and the execution and analysis requirements needed to support an answer at the bottom."}

Read @fig-moonshot-prompt from top to bottom. The compact prompt names the
workload, ISA basis, compute alternatives, power and process envelope, and
requested report. The middle layer expands those phrases into workload,
software, hardware, memory, physical, reliability, and verification
requirements. The lower layer turns those requirements into represented study
state, methods and tools, evidence, and decision support. Architect
judgment can redirect the study at each layer. The figure therefore describes
the hidden work behind the prompt, not a prompt-to-chip automation pipeline.

### Expanding the Lighthouse Requirements {#sec-why-the-prompt-spans-the-stack}

The prompt occupies only a few lines, but answering it requires choices about the workload, software contract, compute organization, memory, power, compiler, runtime, physical design, reliability, and verification (@fig-moonshot-prompt). The bottom panel of the figure shows the work required to connect those choices to tools, evidence, and an architectural decision.

```{=latex}
\FloatBarrier
```

Start with the prompt itself. High-level intent first becomes questions and coupled design choices, not a generated chip artifact. The prompt tasks the architect with comparing several compute organizations for a real-time mobile XR workload, all while respecting a 3\ W TDP[^fn-tdp-c01] budget and the limits of an LP process. Individual phrases bound different parts of the study.

[^fn-tdp-c01]: **TDP (thermal design power)**: Vendors use this term in different ways. This book treats the Lighthouse target as a 3\ W sustained thermal envelope that the declared form factor and cooling assumptions must be able to remove, rather than as a peak instantaneous draw.

The phrase "64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem" fixes the word length and
ISA family. Each study must still choose the exact ISA extensions,
ABI[^fn-abi-c01], compiler, runtime, and software contract. The "XRBench-class
real-time mobile XR workload" specification sets the target environment. The
"accelerator block" provision leaves several compute organizations open for
comparison. Finally, the 3\ W target and 3\ nm-class LP process supply hard
physical limits that can rule out an unfeasible proposal. A 3\ W TDP in a
mobile XR form factor requires the study to state its cooling and
skin-temperature assumptions, packaging, signaling, and the share of the power
budget available to the proposed compute subsystem.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **ABI (application binary interface)**: The binary-level agreement on register usage, calling conventions, stack layout, and data alignment that lets separately compiled code interoperate. Adding a custom instruction changes the ISA, but shipping it means the compiler, libraries, and operating system have to agree on the ABI as well, which is why an ISA extension is a software project rather than a hardware edit.

While the prompt asks for a design-space report, the study may also produce software, models, RTL, layouts, prototypes, or a physical chip, depending on the ambition of the claim. The report connects those artifacts and measurements to the proposed design and explains precisely why alternatives were rejected. To test the architect's judgment, the prompt deliberately leaves the accelerator microarchitecture, memory system, software integration, and evaluation tools open.

Turning those choices into a study requires formal constraints. Requirement translation already combines profiling, analytical models, prior designs, design tools, and expert judgment. A product request such as "we need a low-power AR headset" does not determine a 3\ W TDP, a particular RISC-V extension, or an L2 capacity on its own. The architect must derive those study parameters from workload and system evidence.

Learned methods can assist by extracting candidate constraints from requirement documents, relating them to prior designs and public benchmarks, and identifying ambiguities for the architect to resolve. When a prompt asks for a "real-time" workload, a language model might ask whether that means a strict 11 millisecond frame deadline at 90\ Hz, a 20 millisecond motion-to-photon bound, or a 99th-percentile tail-latency target.

This assistance does not remove the architect's formulation work. It may reduce the time spent assembling candidate specifications, while the architect still decides whether the proposed bounds are complete and supported. Before search begins, the accepted constraints should be represented in a form the relevant tools can use, such as a parameterized generator configuration or a sweep specification. Prose alone cannot define the legal design space.

Each fragment of the Lighthouse prompt implies a cluster of architectural
decisions and the checks that could disqualify an answer
(@tbl-moonshot-decomposition). AI may
suggest a hardware and software decomposition. The architect accepts, revises,
or rejects that proposed scope and its coupled interfaces.

| **Prompt fragment** | **Architectural decisions** | **What must be checked** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **XRBench mobile XR** | Workload slice, input distribution, quality-of-service target, latency deadline, memory traffic, software pipeline, and drift assumptions. | Trace source, benchmark version, documented workload-phase selection, and rejection when results over-optimize a single hot loop or miss real-time behavior. |
| **64-bit RISC-V with vector or accelerator option** | ISA boundary, custom extension policy, programming model, compiler/runtime path, library support, and software compatibility. | Correctness, toolchain support, generated-code evidence, portability checks, and rejection of unsupported software semantics. |
| **Compute subsystem** | CPU, vector, or accelerator organization; memory hierarchy and interconnect; system integration; interface compatibility; and relevant reliability or isolation assumptions. | Design-space comparison and rejection of candidates that only win by moving cost, bandwidth, energy, complexity, or risk elsewhere. |
| **3\ W, 3\ nm-class low-power envelope** | Power, voltage and frequency, thermal and area limits, implementation constraints, and the hardware and software interfaces used for power management. | Source, version, and calibration of the power model; physical-design limits such as voltage drop, wire reliability, and timing closure; sensitivity analysis; and rejection criteria for throttling or reliability failures. |
| **Design-space report with evidence and rejected alternatives** | Alternatives, the Pareto frontier (the set of objective outcomes of feasible designs for which no alternative is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on at least one) [@Deb2001MultiObjective], assumptions, uncertainty, verification plan, rejected or failed candidates, and points at which the responsible architect decides whether to continue. | Measurements linked to assumptions and checks, rejected candidates, coverage, reproducible artifacts, and a named person responsible for the recommendation. |

: **What each prompt fragment requires.** The Lighthouse prompt maps to decisions about workload definition, software and ISA contracts, hardware organization, physical feasibility, and evidence. {#tbl-moonshot-decomposition tbl-colwidths="[18,34,35]"}

Read each row from left to right. The prompt fragment fixes one part of the
challenge, the middle column names the design choices still open, and the last
column names the checks that can disqualify an answer. Read the rows together
as well, because a workload, software, hardware, or physical choice can change
the validity of the others. The table is a requirements expansion rather than
a complete specification. An answer is incomplete if it cannot identify its workload
slice, software contract, physical assumptions, supporting observations, or
decision owner.

Each row points to engineering depth that the short prompt leaves unstated. To verify whether a candidate actually fits the "3\ W, 3\ nm-class" constraint, the architect needs results from RTL, synthesis, floorplanning, timing, IR drop, leakage, thermal analysis, and final signoff. Comparing the RISC-V vector and accelerator alternatives requires checking the compiler, runtime, libraries, generated code, and software portability. Crucially, the hardest bottleneck is often the software stack. A novel spatial accelerator is dead silicon if the compiler cannot be co-adapted to target it. The Lighthouse prompt is therefore a computer architecture problem rather than a prompt engineering exercise, demanding an answer that connects decisions and evidence across the stack.

The workload and process phrases require more detail than the compact prompt provides. The XRBench suite supplies a concrete workload anchor rather than a vague application label. End-to-end XR research shows how tightly perception and display stages are coupled, making mobile XR a system-level architecture target rather than a single kernel to optimize [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR]. AI can help here by analyzing dataset distributions to find coverage gaps, complementing profiling, trace analysis, and expert workload judgment. For instance, a model could ingest the XRBench memory trace and automatically cluster access patterns to recommend specific cache hierarchies or local scratchpads before any simulation begins.

The selected benchmark must strictly represent the system claim. Similarly, the process node is stated as a broad class rather than a named foundry process design kit (PDK)[^fn-pdk-c01]. Even though 2024 mobile SoCs were publicly described in 3\ nm-class technology, the study must explicitly name the process, libraries, voltage assumptions, and signoff path [@Apple2024A18Pro; @Apple2024M4]. Each surviving candidate is then evaluated in a physical harness that applies PPA and static timing limits.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **PDK (process design kit)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. Open PDKs exist, but the authorized models and libraries for an advanced commercial process may be proprietary, so a public corpus cannot substitute for the project-specific process information used by the tool flow.

The Lighthouse prompt fixes the workload class, 64-bit RISC-V basis, permitted
compute organizations, 3\ W envelope, 3\ nm-class low-power process, and
required design-space report. Each study must still specify the workload
version, trace, slice, and deadline; the architecture and software path; the
reference design; the process libraries and operating assumptions; and the
tools, budget, stopping rules, and checks. Those study choices may vary.
Changing the fixed conditions means answering a different challenge.

Meeting those requirements calls for a coordinated technical system, not one
model at the center of a prompt-to-chip pipeline. The system must maintain
current project knowledge, combine learned and conventional methods, connect
those methods to compilers, simulators, implementation tools, and verification,
and return results that can be checked independently of the method that
produced the candidate. The architect remains outside that technical boundary:
framing the intent and constraints, choosing how the components are combined,
reviewing what the checks establish, and making the consequential design
decision.

In this book, an *architecture foundation model* means one broadly pretrained
learned component intended for adaptation across multiple architecture tasks.
It may supply reusable prior knowledge, but it does not contain authoritative
live project state and is not a complete design system. We use *architecture
foundation system* sparingly for the coordinated technical ensemble of learned
and conventional components, tools, maintained state, feedback, and checks. A
particular problem may use one foundation model, several specialized models,
or no foundation model at all. The moonshot is the capability of the complete
system and the architects who use it, not the name or scale of any one model.

## An Artifact Is Not an Architecture Result

An architect might begin with an XRBench trace slice and software pipeline, propose vector-width or CPU and accelerator alternatives, and screen them with a cheap proxy. The architect can then reserve scarce compiler, simulator, RTL, or physical-design feedback for the candidates whose results could actually alter the final decision. That selection rule, along with what the resulting evidence may support, should be stated before the run.

Architecture work moves through a sequence that should not be collapsed:
request, requirements, specification, candidate artifacts, measurements and
checks, comparative architecture result, and decision. An *artifact* is
something produced during the work, such as code, RTL, a configuration, a
model, a layout, a report, or a testbench. A *candidate* is a proposed design
or configuration being compared. A *measurement* or *observation* is
information obtained about a candidate under stated conditions. An
*architecture result* is a supported comparison or finding whose assumptions,
conditions, checks, alternatives, and limits are clear enough to inform a
decision. An architecture result can reject every candidate, retain the
current design, narrow the question, or conclude that the available
measurements cannot decide.

The distance between an artifact and a result is especially large in hardware.
A generator might produce a mathematically elegant instruction extension that
passes behavioral simulation and still fail logic equivalence checking,
design-rule checks, timing, power, or thermal limits in implementation. A
surrogate model[^fn-surrogate-model-c01] can cheaply screen candidates, but a
candidate selected by the surrogate may fail when a more faithful tool exposes
a property the surrogate did not represent. This is the architecture version
of the simulation-to-real problem studied in machine learning
[@TobinEtAl2017DomainRandomization].

[^fn-surrogate-model-c01]: **Surrogate model**: A cheap, data-driven stand-in for an expensive simulator that lets a method screen many candidates quickly. Its score is only a proxy, so a promising candidate still needs a higher-fidelity check before it can support a design decision.

A concise rationale should connect proposals, tool results, rejected
alternatives, and the recommendation, but the rationale is not itself a
measurement. Its purpose is to help a reviewer find missing assumptions,
contradictions, or conclusions that the checks do not support.

Before any simulator runs, Amdahl's law supplies a rejection check for free. An accelerator that covers 60 percent of the XR pipeline's cycles caps whole-system speedup at 2.5 times, no matter how fast the block itself becomes [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. A generated candidate whose profiled coverage cannot support its claimed system gain is ruled out by arithmetic alone, before it consumes a single simulator hour. The first question to put to a generator-proposed design is therefore not how fast the block is but how much of the workload it actually touches.

The roofline model supplies a second screening bound by relating arithmetic
intensity to peak compute and memory bandwidth [@Williams2009Roofline].

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The roofline rejects a candidate before the simulator sees it"}
**Context.** Architects own a second free screen, and this one supplies a bound rather than a ceiling. The model bounds a kernel's attainable performance by its arithmetic intensity, set against the machine's peak compute and memory bandwidth.

**In the XR pipeline.** One profile of the pipeline's flops per byte tells us which candidates are bandwidth-bound before a single line of RTL exists, so wider vector units on a starved kernel can be rejected on the back of an envelope. A proposal the roofline already rules out should never reach the simulator queue.
:::

Within that screening workflow, generation might produce legal vector configurations, prediction might estimate their data-movement risks, and optimization might choose which configurations merit expensive evaluation. A proxy may rank candidates one way, a simulator may overturn that ranking, and an EDA run may return timing paths and congestion rather than a single score.

This work immediately hits the cost of evaluation. A cycle-accurate hardware
simulation or physical implementation run can be substantially slower and more
resource-intensive than a software unit test, and access may be limited by
shared tool queues. Iterative search may require many trials before it can
distinguish better actions. When each trial requires one of these checks, a
brute-force approach quickly exceeds the available budget. Expensive checks
must be reserved for candidates that merit them, but search can then
overfit[^fn-overfitting-c01] the convenient fast proxy used for screening.

[^fn-overfitting-c01]: **Overfitting**: The machine-learning failure of fitting the noise of a training sample so closely that performance does not generalize to new data. An optimizer can overfit a proxy the same way, raising the measured score by exploiting the proxy's quirks rather than improving the true objective.

The same problem appears over a longer time horizon. Software models can
change in weeks, while a design started today may not ship in silicon for
years. An optimizer cannot safely specialize a 3\ nm-class accelerator to one
static trace without considering how workloads and software may change before
deployment. The architect must balance specialization with enough
programmability to survive that delay.

While these methods narrow the work, their output alone does not prove whether a compiler assumption holds, whether the measured behavior follows from the proposed mechanism, or whether the remaining tradeoff justifies a multimillion-dollar commitment. The final evidence should document the candidates, assumptions, measurements, and rejections that affect the claim without needing every internal model trace. The architect must resolve the remaining questions using this curated body of evidence.

These distinctions set the threshold for a useful result. The measurements
must support a comparison
under stated conditions, the required checks were run and support the
conclusion, important alternatives and failures are recorded, and the result
can inform or close an architecture decision. Rejecting a candidate, retaining
the current architecture, or choosing a conventional method can all be useful
results.

Useful results do not need to cover the whole Lighthouse challenge. Progress
can close one clearly stated part without claiming an end-to-end answer. A
full-scope result addresses the complete challenge and may still conclude that
no candidate works. Full Lighthouse success requires a supported design that
meets the fixed conditions and the complete design-space report promised by the
prompt, including the software path, physical constraints, rejected
alternatives, checks, and a recommendation an independent architect can
examine.

These judgments also require two different comparisons. A reference design
shows whether one architecture is preferable to another. A credible
conventional or human-directed process shows whether AI improved the work used
to reach the result. The two comparisons are not interchangeable.

### Efficiency Claims Must Be Scoped {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

Even if an AI-assisted process can produce a candidate and a polished report,
an efficiency claim still requires a scoped system comparison. The difference
between a plausible candidate and a defensible design is especially clear
here, because the Lighthouse subsystem cannot be judged from one score.
Workload behavior, software support, data movement, physical limits,
verification effort, and deployment conditions can all change which design is
preferable.

Efficiency is a strict claim about how well a particular architecture performs useful work with limited resources. The claim must name the exact design, workload, and resource budget it covers. A faster design fails to solve the problem if it exceeds the power budget, cannot be verified, or depends on fragile software assumptions.

Efficiency now spans far more than performance and power. Classical computer architecture made performance quantitative while treating cost and power as first-class constraints [@HennessyPatterson2017QuantitativeApproach]. Dennard-style scaling once made it easier to improve performance while keeping power density manageable [@DennardEtAl1974Scaling]. When that scaling regime weakened, dark silicon and the limits of multicore scaling pushed the field toward specialization [@BorkarChien2011FutureMicroprocessors; @EsmaeilzadehEtAl2011DarkSilicon; @HennessyPatterson2019GoldenAge].

The energy cost of data movement soon made arithmetic alone an incomplete
measure. In the cited 45\ nm data, a 32-bit integer add costs about 0.1\ pJ,
the SRAM examples range from 10 to 100\ pJ, and a DRAM access costs 1.3 to
2.6\ nJ [@Horowitz2014Energy]. These values do not determine the Lighthouse
result at a newer process node. They show why data movement can dominate and
why any accelerator that adds DRAM traffic needs an explicit system energy
comparison rather than a compute-only claim.

Warehouse-scale operation expanded the boundary to include power delivery,
utilization, networking, operations, and total cost of ownership
[@BarrosoHolzleRanganathan2019DatacenterAsComputer]. Today, sustainability
adds operational and embodied carbon to the comparison, factors that depend
heavily on energy use, hardware manufacturing, utilization, geography, and
system lifetime [@GuptaEtAl2021ChasingCarbon]. An AI-assisted comparison must
state the assumptions and measurements relevant to each efficiency dimension
and name the violations, such as design-rule-check (DRC) failures or thermal
limits, that immediately rule out a candidate.

A valid comparison must also account for failed and rejected alternatives, not
only the winners. Keeping those results prevents later architects from
reevaluating candidates that earlier evidence ruled out. It also shows
which parts of the design space the claim actually covers.

Modern benchmark suites already reflect this broader view. MLPerf, a community
effort to make machine-learning performance claims reproducible across
systems, includes deployment scenario, latency, throughput, and accuracy in its
comparisons [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. Useful work must be evaluated
against the resource that is scarce in the stated setting, whether that is
latency, throughput, energy, power, area, cost, carbon, reliability,
verification effort, engineering time, or risk.

The design, workload, scenario, and scarce resource together define what
"efficient" means. For the Lighthouse system, a candidate that improves average
throughput may still be a poor choice if it misses an XR frame deadline, exceeds
the 3\ W envelope under sustained load, or adds verification work that the
project cannot absorb. Changing any of those conditions changes the claim and
the evidence needed to support it.

The comparison separates five dimensions of the architecture result from one
dimension of the study used to reach it (@tbl-efficiency-dimensions). An
architect should select the dimensions that define the claim. Reading the rows
together also shows where a gain may shift cost or risk elsewhere.

| **Dimension** | **Efficiency question** | **Why it complicates the comparison** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Performance** | How much useful work is delivered per unit time, latency budget, or service-level target? | The answer depends on workload selection, scenario, software stack, and whether the measured behavior matches the deployment claim. |
| **Power and energy** | How much useful work is delivered per watt, joule, thermal budget, or battery envelope? | A credible comparison must account for activity, data movement, voltage/frequency choices, thermal constraints, and fidelity gaps between estimates and signoff. |
| **Reliability and correctness** | How much useful work survives faults, corner cases, nondeterminism, and validation? | A faster candidate is not efficient if it spends its savings on fragility, security side-channels, debug burden, or invalid software and hardware assumptions. |
| **Scalability and cost** | How much useful work is delivered per dollar, rack, network hop, operator action, or unit of capacity? | Local wins can shift cost to memory, network, power delivery, utilization, operations, or total cost of ownership. |
| **Sustainability** | How much useful work is delivered per unit of operational and embodied environmental footprint? | Carbon depends on hardware lifetime, manufacturing, energy mix, utilization, and where and when computation runs. |
| **Evidence and engineering effort** | How much decision-relevant evidence is obtained per simulation, experiment, verification run, or engineer-hour? | Generating more candidates can still be inefficient if evaluation consumes scarce feedback, hides failures, or cannot reject weak outputs. |

: **Efficiency includes the architecture result and the work needed to establish it:** five dimensions describe the proposed system, while evidence cost describes the study; a valid comparison must show when an apparent improvement shifts cost or changes the scope. {#tbl-efficiency-dimensions tbl-colwidths="[22,32,34]"}

Two kinds of efficiency operate in this comparison. The proposed hardware system must perform useful work within its resource limits, and the study itself must allocate simulator runs, physical-design experiments, verification effort, and expert review carefully enough to reach a reliable conclusion. Reducing the cost of the study is valuable only when the remaining observations can still distinguish the alternatives and expose the failures that matter to the decision.

These efficiency dimensions interact. In the mobile XR setting anchored by XRBench and ILLIXR, frame latency, energy, sustained power, and data movement are so tightly coupled that a gain in one can violate a deadline or thermal limit in another. Better simulated performance can be offset by added verification work, and lower energy may depend on fragile software assumptions. A candidate that wins under a proxy may fail on a more faithful workload. The architect must explain which tradeoffs are acceptable for the stated constraints, defining the scope of the efficiency claim instead of relying on a single attractive artifact or score.

These coupled requirements do not imply that every architecture project needs
AI. Conventional architecture methods may remain preferable when the design
question and permitted change are narrow enough to evaluate directly and the
required feedback is cheap and dependable. We should first identify what
familiar models, scripts, simulators, and expert reviews already handle well
before stating exactly what we expect AI to improve. The test is whether the
assistance leads to a better system or a more reliable conclusion, rather than
simply generating more artifacts.

A common objection is that today's models hallucinate and cannot be trusted to
produce correct hardware, so an AI-assisted architecture program is premature.
The reliability concern is valid, but no architecture method should be trusted
without checks. The practical question is whether the method and its required
checks improve the architecture result, lower the total cost of reaching a
result of comparable quality, or both, relative to competent conventional
work. If every bad proposal requires a multi-hour synthesis run, evaluation can
consume more engineering time and computation than the method saves.

The Lighthouse prompt makes this friction concrete. The requested subsystem must support a workload class, meet a strict power envelope, fit a technology assumption, interact correctly with software, and produce reviewable evidence. The final comparison must weigh energy, latency, memory traffic, programmability, verification, and deployment risk. While a single scalar objective may help an automated search navigate the space, it cannot substitute for architectural judgment.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{11\baselineskip}
```

### What Current Systems Establish

Reading today's tools by what they establish and what remains untested reveals
both rapid progress and persistent gaps. This section does not survey the
field. What follows is a curated set of flagship results, chosen because their successes
and limits are especially diagnostic of where AI-assisted architecture stands.

Different readers can apply that comparison through their own work.

- **Researcher:** Name the architecture question, the role AI played, the
  artifact or finding produced, and the evidence and limits behind it.
- **Tool builder:** Ask whether the harness keeps the inputs, settings,
  results, failures, and costs that another method or engineer would need.
- **Author or reviewer:** Ask what would reject the claim, why the measured
  mechanism supports it, and which decision it can justify.

Begin outside architecture, with the result that sets the frame. AlphaTensor searched the space of matrix-multiplication algorithms and found one that multiplies 4 by 4 matrices in 47 scalar multiplications, improving on the 49 of Strassen's two-level method for the first time in half a century [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor]. Two qualifications travel with that number, and neither is a footnote. The record holds in modular arithmetic over the field of two elements rather than over the reals, and the standard-arithmetic improvements arrived at other matrix shapes. Those qualifications determine where the algorithm applies, so dropping them changes the claim rather than merely simplifying it. Every candidate decomposition admitted an exact algebraic check, and a single scalar counted the multiplications, so invalid candidates were inexpensive to discard relative to a physical design study. Complete architecture claims rarely have one check with the same scope, cost, and decisiveness. Read the rest of this section by asking how evaluation cost, fidelity, task scope, and access to evidence limit what each result establishes.

Inside architecture, tensor-program autotuning approaches that regime. Predictive design-space exploration uses simulated performance to train surrogate models that estimate behavior across a specified design space [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. AutoTVM uses measured hardware execution to guide a statistical search for tensor-program schedules [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. In each case, the input, architecture job, feedback source, and result scope remain clear. AutoTVM operates in a setting where many candidate schedules can run on real hardware quickly and most failures remain contained within the tuning run. That property makes the search practical, but it also limits what the result says about the rest of the system.

AlphaChip, a learning-based macro-placement method, is a prominent
physical-design example. Its inputs are a netlist and macro descriptions, its
job is macro placement, and its feedback comes from proxy rewards such as
wirelength and congestion [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. Its reported
placement speed established how fast the method produces a candidate, not that
it beats strong classical baselines, and its reported deployment across
several TPU generations [@GoogleDeepMind2024AlphaChip;
@GoldieEtAl2024AlphaChipAddendum] is relevant evidence without settling that
matched comparison. The later treatment of feedback and verification examines
the proxy-metric and baseline dispute in full.

Where the feedback is a simulator rather than silicon, the harness starts to matter more than the searcher. ArchGym placed a family of architecture simulators behind one interface and gave competing search algorithms equal sample budgets, finding that no algorithm dominates across design spaces [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. That is a finding about experimental design rather than about any optimizer, and it inherits every fidelity limit of the simulators sitting behind it. Two learned design-space explorations bracket what such evidence can be made to carry. Apollo showed sample-efficient transfer across related design spaces inside one company's accelerator template, evaluated against fast proxies [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo]. BOOM-Explorer found efficient microarchitectures of an open-source RISC-V core through a documented 7\ nm VLSI flow, where hours per sample cap the space it can afford to see [@BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer]. The pair is worth holding together because both show the value of costly, domain-specific evidence while neither supplies a completely public, independently reproducible industrial study.

Generation methods have begun to reach real hardware in narrow settings. In a conversational study, a language model drafted the Verilog for a small 8-bit processor that reached tapeout, though a human guided the model through many revisions [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat]. A separate method that learns a CPU's logic from input-output examples produced a RISC-V core, Enlightenment-1, that was fabricated and runs Linux, reaching that result through a non-agentic search rather than a tool-using loop [@ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU]. Each reaches silicon on a narrow slice of the problem. Among the public systems reviewed here, none carries a full architecture study autonomously from intent to fabricated hardware. Measuring generation ability has itself become standard practice. VerilogEval primarily checks functional behavior on shared RTL tasks, while RTLLM adds post-synthesis design-quality metrics without reaching placed-and-routed physical signoff [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. A later VerilogEval study reports rapid model progress, prompt sensitivity, benchmark revisions, and a more detailed failure classification [@PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval].

Industrial deployment tells a different story from the academic record, and it is harder to read. Domain-adapted models trained on proprietary design data outperform much larger general models on several internal assistance tasks, including engineering question answering, bug triage, and simple EDA scripting [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo]. Their evidence combines expert ratings, task-specific measures, and functional checks on simple scripts, which suggests a near-term industrial shape of an assistant beside the flow rather than an agent inside it. A language-model agent can also plan and drive a real synthesis-to-layout tool flow from natural-language intent, though it orchestrates existing tools on small designs and its correctness rides entirely on the tools it calls [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA]. Learned search over flow parameters has crossed into commercial use, with 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts [@Synopsys2023DSOai]. That last claim is the one to sit with. Its evidence standard is a press release, with no public methodology, no baseline, and no matched comparison, and it is nonetheless among the most widely repeated evidence that this technology works at scale.

The pattern across all of them is easier to see side by side (@tbl-existing-systems). Reading down the limits column reveals several different constraints on the claim, including check cost and fidelity, task scope, baseline quality, workflow coverage, and whether an outside reviewer can inspect the evidence.

| **System** | **What it establishes** | **The telltale limit** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AlphaTensor [@FawziEtAl2022AlphaTensor] | Learned search can pass a fifty-year human frontier and prove the result correct | The check is exact, inexpensive, and algebraic, and one scalar scores it |
| AutoTVM [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM] | Measured search can improve schedules when many candidates run quickly on real hardware | The result covers tensor-program schedules, where failures are usually contained within the tuning run |
| AlphaChip [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement; @ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment] | A learned policy produces macro placements a production flow accepts | The reward is proxy wirelength and congestion, and the matched baseline is disputed |
| ArchGym [@KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym] | At equal sample budgets no search algorithm dominates, so the harness and budget shape the result | Every candidate is graded by a simulator, so the result inherits its fidelity limits |
| Apollo and BOOM-Explorer [@yazdanbakhsh2021apollo; @BaiEtAl2021BOOMExplorer] | Learned design-space exploration can exploit domain-specific evidence | Apollo scores fast proxies inside one firm's template; BOOM-Explorer uses an open-source core but depends on commercial tools and pays hours per sample |
| VerilogEval and RTLLM [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM] | RTL generation is measurable on shared tasks | VerilogEval emphasizes functional simulation; RTLLM adds post-synthesis quality metrics; neither reaches physical signoff |
| Chip-Chat and Enlightenment-1 [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat; @ChengEtAl2024AutomatedCPU] | Generated logic has reached silicon, in one case a core that boots Linux | A human drove one and a non-agentic search the other, so no autonomous loop reached silicon |
| ChatEDA [@HeEtAl2024ChatEDA] | An agent can plan and invoke a real tool flow from stated intent | It drives existing tools on small designs, so correctness rides on the tools it calls |
| ChipNeMo [@LiuEtAl2023ChipNeMo] | Domain-adapted models beat far larger general models on several internal assistance tasks | The evidence combines expert ratings, task-specific measures, and simple script checks, and none of it is externally reproducible |
| DSO.ai [@Synopsys2023DSOai] | Learned flow-parameter search has reached 100 vendor-reported commercial tapeouts | The evidence standard is a press release, with no public methodology or matched baseline |

: **The strength of each result depends on its scope and how it was evaluated:** Exact, inexpensive checks support strong scoped claims, while narrow measurements, proxies, weak baselines, and supporting data, methods, or artifacts that outsiders cannot inspect each limit what an architect can conclude. {#tbl-existing-systems tbl-colwidths="[20,37,43]"}

These tools succeed at their individual tasks while exposing the integration problem that a whole architecture study must solve. Adjacent fields faced a version of it and moved forward by adopting shared baselines, standardized datasets, and common evaluation. ImageNet [@RussakovskyEtAl2015ImageNet] gave computer vision a common benchmark, and CASP (Critical Assessment of Structure Prediction) [@MoultEtAl1995CASP] let AlphaFold's [@JumperEtAl2021AlphaFold] structure predictions be measured against community-held standards. Computer architecture needs the same shared tasks, public datasets, and open evaluation protocols to turn narrow tool use into a reviewable AI-assisted practice.

Progress toward the moonshot will require more than isolated demonstrations. Software engineering offers a useful contrast because it can often obtain a task-level result much faster than hardware design can obtain physical evidence. SWE-bench turns real GitHub-issue fixes into a shared task graded by automated repository tests, giving coding agents a relatively quick and repeatable signal (@fig-swebench-progress) [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench]. Passing those tests does not prove complete software correctness, but it supports a specific claim about resolving the issue under the benchmark conditions. Hardware also has fast checks for specific properties. A complete system-and-chip claim, however, must connect functional verification with synthesis, timing, power, physical-design, and thermal evidence whose cost and fidelity differ.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swebench-progress
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Standardized task-level checks support rapid iteration on SWE-bench Verified.** Best reported SWE-bench Verified score [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] for each model name in a dated snapshot of Epoch AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; the line traces the best result to date. Reported configurations and test harnesses can differ, so the plot shows the pace of benchmark progress rather than a controlled comparison among models. Scores climbed from roughly a third of this human-filtered 500-task subset to over four-fifths in about seventeen months. Repository tests provide a quick, repeatable signal for the defined task, while a complete architecture claim must combine functional and physical evidence from several tools.
#| out-width: "88%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter of the best reported SWE-bench Verified resolved percentage for each model name versus model release date from late 2024 to 2026. Points climb from about 31 percent to about 84 percent, with a solid line tracing the best-to-date frontier."

import csv
import datetime
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

# Data: SWE-bench Verified results [@JimenezEtAl2024SWEBench] tracked in Epoch
# AI's benchmarking hub [@EpochAI2025AIModels]; best score per model name in
# the dated snapshot. Values dataset-transcribed. Accessed 2026-07-19.
# Receipt: data/source-receipts/chapter1-swebench-verified.csv
_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]

def _yfrac(text):
    for fmt in ("%Y-%m-%d", "%Y-%m", "%Y"):
        try:
            d = datetime.datetime.strptime(text.strip(), fmt)
            return d.year + (d.timetuple().tm_yday - 1) / 365.25
        except ValueError:
            continue
    return None

pts = []
with open(_root / "data" / "source-receipts" / "chapter1-swebench-verified.csv", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for row in csv.DictReader(fh):
        x = _yfrac(row["release_date"])
        try:
            score = float(row["resolved_fraction"])
        except ValueError:
            continue
        if x is None:
            continue
        pts.append({"model": row["model"], "score": score * 100 if score <= 1 else score, "x": x})

# The snapshot can contain several configurations under the same model name.
# Retain only the best reported score for each name rather than presenting
# those configurations as distinct model releases.
best_by_name = {}
for p in pts:
    name = (p["model"] or "").strip()
    if name not in best_by_name or p["score"] > best_by_name[name]["score"]:
        best_by_name[name] = p
pts = list(best_by_name.values())
pts.sort(key=lambda p: p["x"])
best = -1.0
frontier = []
for p in pts:
    if p["score"] > best:
        best = p["score"]
        frontier.append(p)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.4, 3.2))
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in pts], [p["score"] for p in pts], s=16, marker="o",
           facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.7, zorder=2, label="Named models")
ax.plot([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], color=COLORS["evidence"], lw=1.6, zorder=3)
ax.scatter([p["x"] for p in frontier], [p["score"] for p in frontier], s=22, marker="o",
           facecolor=COLORS["evidence"], edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=0.5, zorder=4, label="Best to date")
ax.set_xlim(2024.8, 2026.55)
ax.set_ylim(20, 92)
ax.set_xlabel("Model release date", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_ylabel("SWE-bench Verified resolved (%)", fontsize=7.2)
ax.set_xticks([2025.0, 2025.5, 2026.0, 2026.5])
ax.set_xticklabels(["2025", "mid-25", "2026", "mid-26"], fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=6.4, length=2.5, width=0.6)
for _sp in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_sp].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(True, which="major", axis="y", color=COLORS["row"], linewidth=0.4, zorder=0)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False, fontsize=6.0, handletextpad=0.3, labelspacing=0.3)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.97, top=0.98, bottom=0.12)
```

The horizontal axis covers roughly seventeen months of model releases, while
the vertical axis reports the share of SWE-bench Verified issues resolved. Each
hollow point is the best result associated with one model name in the dated
snapshot, and the solid line retains only results that set a new reported best.
Because the submitted configurations and test harnesses can differ, the points do
not isolate model quality. The rising frontier instead shows the pace at which
a standardized, automated task-level check can support iteration across models
and engineering systems. Best reported scores rose from roughly a third of the
benchmark issues to over four-fifths. Architecture also uses fast analytical,
structural, and functional checks, but no single one closes a complete
system-and-chip claim. Timing closure, design rules, power targets, and thermal
limits require later and more expensive evidence. Fast static analysis and
calibrated proxies can reduce that cost by screening candidates, but they do
not replace the implementation checks on which a physical claim depends.

SPEC-style benchmarks made performance claims more comparable by specifying workloads, run rules, and reporting standards, and a benchmark that becomes standard also steers which improvements a community goes after [@Patterson2012Benchmarks]. SPEC CPU defines common workloads and reporting rules [@SPEC2017CPU]. gem5 supplies a shared simulation platform [@BinkertEtAl2011Gem5], FireSim supplies an FPGA-accelerated simulation platform [@KarandikarEtAl2018FireSim], and MLPerf defines benchmark suites and submission rules for machine-learning systems [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf]. These resources do not make results automatically correct, but they give other researchers common objects with which to rerun, compare, and challenge a claim. AI-assisted results will need the same shared tasks, tool interfaces, and evidence standards to matter beyond a single study.

### Data Scarcity and the Verification Load {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

If these systems and tools are so promising, why is AI-assisted architecture not a solved problem? Two forces hold it back, and both trace to how little hardware design data reaches the open world and how much of the remaining work is verification. The first force has a name, *dark data*, design knowledge that exists in volume inside companies but never reaches any public corpus.

Software and hardware differ in what public repositories expose. Software
corpora can draw on source changes, technical discussions, and tests from
public projects. Architecture corpora cannot include proprietary hardware IP,
advanced commercial process models, or production silicon data without
authorization. The public record therefore leaves important gaps between RTL
or architecture choices and outcomes such as power-delivery routing or
advanced-node timing. A generator trained largely on public text may reproduce
plausible syntax without representing project-specific constraints, so its
outputs still require constraint-aware representations and appropriate tool
checks.

A method need not infer every physical constraint from training data. An
architect can supply specifications and analytical models, encode formal
constraints in the representation, retrieve current documentation, or use
tool results to revise a candidate. Tool-guided repair after a syntax or
compiler error is one route [@TsaiEtAl2024RTLFixer], but each route exposes
different information and has different costs. Open hardware resources also
help in different ways. Chipyard connects shareable RISC-V-based designs to
simulation and implementation paths [@chipyard], while OpenROAD provides an
open digital physical-design flow [@AjayiEtAl2019OpenROAD]. They complement
proprietary data, domain adaptation, synthetic examples, and physics-based
models rather than serving as the only route. Their restricted coverage raises
the value of sample-efficient methods, better representations, and explicit
constraints.

Scarce data also raises the verification stakes. A model that cannot generate correct hardware zero-shot[^fn-zero-shot-c01] may emit plausible but subtly flawed structures, and industry data shows that verification consumes roughly half of total project engineering effort, with design engineers spending about half their time in verification [@Foster2022WilsonVerificationStudy]. If a generator produces thousands of novel accelerators a day but engineers must manually write UVM[^fn-uvm-c01] testbenches for them, it has moved the limiting work to verification. Producing candidates faster than reviewers can check them deepens that backlog, so formal-verification tools and constrained-random testing remain part of the work rather than an afterthought. A generated cache controller that hides a coherence deadlock is worse than useless if the deadlock takes months to find. The cost of a defect can rise sharply when it escapes into later validation stages or fabricated silicon. This escalation makes early analytical, functional, formal, and physical checks economically important.

[^fn-zero-shot-c01]: **Zero-shot generation**: Producing an output for a task without task-specific examples or iterative feedback. A first-pass RTL result still requires checks against the design specification and implementation constraints. Examples, retrieved knowledge, explicit constraints, domain adaptation, and tool-guided revision can all improve later attempts.

[^fn-uvm-c01]: **UVM (Universal Verification Methodology)**: The standard SystemVerilog class library teams use to build constrained-random testbenches, supplying reusable stimulus drivers, monitors, scoreboards, and coverage collectors. The testbench is often larger than the design it checks, so generating hardware faster only helps if the verification collateral scales with it.

Verification must also reach past functional correctness when the design's threat model includes hardware security. Spectre showed that functionally correct processors can still expose microarchitectural side channels [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre]. An AI-assisted study that generates security-relevant hardware must apply independent checks appropriate to the design and threat model, which may include isolation properties, side-channel analysis, or checks for malicious modifications. Generation may help produce SystemVerilog assertions, security properties, and testbenches, but it does not establish its own correctness.

Even when the data exist, a design change stated in one sentence may require
many files and long-running commands before the toolchain returns a result.
The central problem is no longer how to obtain one plausible artifact. It is
how to organize the complete design work so that each action advances a
question and each consequential result can be checked.

## What Changes and What Does Not {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

Architecture 1.0 is shorthand for established, human-directed architecture
practice. It already includes analytical models, scripted flows, automated
search, parameterized generators, simulators, synthesis, optimization, and
verification. Architecture 2.0 retains that foundation while allowing learned
methods to perform selected roles across more of the work
[@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. The distinction is about the breadth
and role of AI participation, not manual work versus automation
(@tbl-arch1-vs-arch2).

| **Feature** | **Established architecture practice (Architecture 1.0)** | **AI-assisted architecture practice (Architecture 2.0)** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Problem framing | Architects define the question, abstractions, constraints, and tool tasks | Learned methods may help interpret broader intent or incomplete information and propose choices for architect review |
| Exploration | Architects use analytical models, scripts, parameterized generators, sweeps, and conventional optimization | Prediction, generation, and learned optimization may propose, screen, or select alternatives alongside established methods |
| Tool use | Architects and scripts invoke simulators and design tools, preserve results, and decide what to run next | Automated components may select later actions from tool returns, so state, cost, failures, and permitted actions must be usable by the component and inspectable by the reviewer |
| Decision making | Architects integrate results and remain responsible for the design decision | Methods may organize analysis or prepare a recommendation, while architects retain responsibility for the design decision |

: **AI participation broadens what may be delegated without changing who owns the decision:** Architecture 2.0 adds learned prediction, generation, optimization, retrieval, or tool coordination to established analytical and automated practice while the architect retains scope, interpretation, and responsibility. {#tbl-arch1-vs-arch2}

Read each row across as a change in who or what may perform the work, not as a
transfer of authority. The first two rows broaden assistance with problem
framing and exploration. The tool-use row adds a practical requirement: an
automated component must be able to use the relevant project state, and a
reviewer must be able to inspect the inputs, actions, costs, and failures on
which the result rests. The final row keeps the design decision with the
architect.

The relevant unit of comparison is therefore the complete design system, not a
model in isolation. It includes the architecture question, represented project
state, methods, conventional algorithms, tools, returned feedback, checks,
human work, total cost, and resulting decision. A local improvement can make
that system worse. A faster generator can enlarge simulator and review queues,
and a cheaper predictor can discard the candidate that a later physical check
would have favored.

AI participation does not create good record keeping automatically.
Conventional projects can and often do preserve inputs, artifact versions,
tool results, rejected candidates, and decisions. Wider automated
participation makes the relevant state necessary both for component action and
for review (@fig-design-loop-breaks).

![**AI participation requires usable design state.** Both studies can record inputs, actions, tool results, rejected candidates, and decisions. When automated components act on that information, it must also be represented where the components can use it and reviewers can inspect it.](images/F2a-design-loop-breaks){#fig-design-loop-breaks width="85%" fig-alt="Two side-by-side diagrams compare human-orchestrated and AI-assisted architecture studies. Both preserve design state and depend on architectural judgment. AI participation additionally requires the relevant inputs, actions, tool results, and decision responsibility to be usable by automated components and inspectable by reviewers."}

Read the left panel as familiar human-orchestrated work. Intent moves through
models and scripts to a candidate, tool feedback, and expert review, while some
state and rationale remain in expert practice. On the right, automated
components also act on represented state and returned feedback. A failed check
can revise the state and redirect the next action, while architect review
remains between the returned information and any consequential commitment.
Making state usable and inspectable does not make the result correct. It makes
the basis of the action available for checking.

## Why Coordination Must Be Deliberate

A collection of capable models and tools is not yet a design method. A short
request leaves requirements and acceptance checks unresolved. As work moves
among documents, intermediate representations, generators, compilers,
simulators, and implementation tools, cross-layer intent can be lost. Reusable
models also have uneven support and stale knowledge, while live project state
changes from one run to the next.

The tools themselves impose another constraint. Simulator runs, synthesis,
physical design, and verification consume time and computation, and they can
fail in ways that plausible text does not reveal. A fast surrogate for timing
or congestion may rank candidates differently from the tools used for
signoff. An optimizer asked only to reduce power may share a resource that the
system isolated for security or reliability. Producing candidates faster can
therefore move the limiting work into checking and review, especially when
the objective omitted a system obligation.

Feedback also needs qualification. Several components may repeat the same
wrong assumption because they share training data, a proxy, or an underlying
model. An *independent check* is sufficiently separate from candidate
production that the producing method cannot determine its result, and its
decisive assumptions and implementation are not simply inherited from the
generator. Complete independence is uncommon, but candidate production and
the checks that decide acceptance must remain separate enough to expose
failure.

Deliberate coordination means organizing the work through a life cycle,
maintaining the required data and current project knowledge, choosing and
combining methods for their assigned roles, connecting them to real
environments, qualifying feedback and verification, evaluating the complete
configuration, and preserving architectural judgment. These are engineering
responsibilities, not names for software modules. They are also the teaching
obligations taken up by the rest of this book.

## Two Independent Tests for the Moonshot

The moonshot must pass two logically distinct comparisons. The first evaluates
the architecture. The second evaluates the contribution made by AI.

**Architecture success.** Does the proposed design meet the fixed Lighthouse
conditions and justify itself against the architecture reference under the
required workload, software, implementation, physical, and verification
checks? The result may be a better design, a supported decision to retain the
reference, or a finding that the available alternatives do not meet the
conditions.

**AI contribution.** Against the strongest practical conventional or
human-directed process with matched starting information, tool access, total
budget, human work accounting, and stopping conditions, did the AI-assisted
approach improve the architecture result, reduce the total cost of reaching a
result of comparable quality, or both?

The distinction has several consequences. A good design does not prove that AI
improved the work. A cheaper process does not justify an inferior design. A
sound conventional result remains a success for the architecture question
even if AI is not the better method. Random search may provide a useful floor,
but it is not automatically the strongest practical conventional comparison.
"Independent" here means that the two tests answer different questions, not
that their measurements are statistically independent.

A broader program assessment can aggregate repeated AI-contribution results
across tasks, design stages, and conditions. It is not a third test equal to
the two above. Under matched conditions, the AI bet has failed within the
assessed program if it repeatedly improves neither the architecture result nor
the total cost of reaching a defensible decision. The public evidence reviewed
for this edition does not yet settle that verdict.

## Open Research Questions

The moonshot leaves four broad questions open. They concern the design
practice that computer architecture needs, not one model or benchmark. Every
chapter closes with open research questions, with each set matched to the
chapter's scope.

### Turning Intent Into a Design Problem

**How can broad system intent become an executable specification without
losing the obligations that determine architecture value?** Workload behavior,
software semantics, interfaces, physical limits, verification, and acceptance
checks must survive the translation from request to tools. The open problem is
not merely extracting more detail from prose; it is knowing which details must
remain coupled and who resolves ambiguity.

### Finding Where AI Creates Net Value

**Which architecture work benefits from learned assistance after all of its
costs are counted?** Data preparation, tool integration, simulation,
verification, review, and failures can outweigh a faster local step. Computer
architecture needs ways to identify where AI can improve the result or reduce
the total cost of reaching a result of comparable quality, and where
established methods remain better.

### Establishing a System Result

**How can an outside reviewer distinguish a plausible artifact from a
supported architecture result and a demonstrated AI contribution?** The
measurements may span tools with different fidelity, cost, and access, while
some design data cannot be published. A credible answer must still show what
improved, what was checked, what remains uncertain, and where cost or risk
moved.

### Building the Enabling System

**What reusable knowledge and components can support many architecture tasks
without becoming detached from the current design?** Reusable prior knowledge
could reduce repeated work, but design state, tools, and constraints change
across projects. The open problem is determining when reuse remains valid and
when it must yield to current, project-specific information.

## Conclusion

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Keep the moonshot testable"}
1. **Treat the request as the beginning, not the specification.** Expand intent
   into the workload, software, hardware, physical, and verification
   obligations that make comparison possible.
2. **Treat artifacts as inputs to judgment, not as results.** A candidate
   becomes an architecture result only when measurements and checks support a
   comparison under stated conditions.
3. **Evaluate the architecture and the AI contribution separately.** A good
   design does not prove that AI improved the work, and a cheaper process does
   not justify an inferior design.
:::

The Lighthouse request gives the moonshot a fixed system-and-chip target
across workload, software, hardware, implementation, physical constraints,
verification, and the final recommendation. A coordinated design system may
use foundation or specialized models, prediction, generation, optimization,
retrieval, conventional algorithms, and tool-connected environments. None of
those components is the moonshot by itself. The capability lies in carrying
the architecture question through the complete work while the architect
frames, reviews, and commits.

The two tests keep that ambition honest. The architecture comparison asks
whether a supported design meets the Lighthouse conditions. The AI comparison
asks whether assistance improves the result, lowers the total cost of reaching
a comparable result, or both. Current systems show meaningful progress on
individual tasks, but their evaluation cost, fidelity, scope, and access to
supporting material limit what they establish about the complete challenge.

With the target and its tests in place, the next question is why present-day
architecture work has become difficult enough that additional assistance is
worth investigating.
